acknowledgement.p: This problem set was developed for the MATH A305 Introduction to Geometries at the University of Alaska Anchorage. It has been modified based on the experience of the students in this class.

preface.p: This text was designed for an IBL approach to MATH A305 Introduction to Geometries at the University of Alaska Anchorage. Its purpose in the mathematics baccalaureates at UAA is to cover geometry topics required for secondary teacher certification. As a result it covers synthetic, transformational, and a tiny bit of analytic approaches to geometry and covers both Euclidean (parabolic), hyperbolic, and some projective geometry.
Students are expected to have completed a proofs course covering proof techniques, basic set operations, and cardinality as a prerequisite. The students have typically taken high school geometry.

section.title: Finite Geometries

statement.p: Two lines intersect if and only if they share a point.
Two lines are parallel if and only if they do not intersect.

The four point geometry is defined by the following axioms and definitions.
There exist exactly four points.
Any two, distinct points have exactly one line on them.
Each line is on exactly two points.

A finite projective geometry satisfies the following conditions.
Any two, distinct points have exactly one line on them.

Construct a projective geometry with exactly 4 points on every line.

We want every line to contain exactly four points. So, we can draw the following lines.
We arrange the lines in this way to not violate axiom 3 of the Finite Projective Geometry. Then, notice we can repeat this pattern as follows.

Once again, we satisfy axiom 3. But, we cannot repeat this pattern again since we would be violating axiom 1. So, we have to come up with a different strategy to connect our top and rightmost points with the rest of the diagram such that we do not violate axiom 1. Instead of attaching the points along the verticals and horizontals, we can attack from the diagonals like so.
If we draw our lines this way, we still satisfy all the axioms. Now, notice we can repeat this same method of attachment on our topmost point.

We see that this final image satisfies the three axioms of the finite projective geometry:

To see how we satisfy axiom 2, we can pick the centermost point, the topmost post, the rightmost point, and the left middle point of the 3\times3 grid. Further, as per the problem statement, each line has exactly four points on it.

This problem follows 1.4.5, where we are asked to modify the axioms of the Nine Point Geometry:
There exists exactly nine points,
There exists exactly nine lines,
Any two distinct points have exactly one line on them,
Each line is on exactly three points.
I followed the following modification to these axioms:
There exists exactly nine points,
Any two distinct points have exactly one line on them,
Each line is on exactly three points.
To visualize this geometry, we first place 9 points in a 3\times 3 grid.
Next, draw 3 horizontal and 3 vertical lines like so to satisfy axiom 3.
Since we need to connect the corners to satisfy axiom 2, draw two diagonal lines.

But, the corners do not connect to the middle edges on the opposing sides. Notice that each corner is not adjacent to exactly two edges. So, we can draw lines that connect each corner to their nonadjacent edge points that will conveniently satisfy axioms 2 and 3.
Now, all axioms are satisfied. There are 12 lines in this depiction of the Nine Point Geometry.

subsection.title: Basic Triangle Theorems
subsection.p: Note all theorems in this section can and should be proved without using the parallel postulate.

statement.p: The opposing angles formed by the intersection of two lines are called vertical angles.
Two angles are congruent (\angle ABC \cong \angle DEF) if and only if their measures are equal (m\angle ABC = m\angle DEF).
Vertical angles are congruent.

image.shortdescription: Image required for the proof of Theorem 2-1-3.

proof.p: Take the figure above. Because angles \alpha and \gamma form a linear pair, the supplement postulate indicates that m(\angle\alpha)+m(\angle\gamma)=180 . We also know that \gamma and \beta form a linear pair, so we know that m(\angle\gamma)+m(\angle\beta)=180 .

Thus, m(\angle\alpha)+m(\angle\gamma)=m(\angle\gamma)+m(\angle\beta) So, m(\angle\alpha)=m(\angle\beta). Thus, \angle\alpha\cong\angle\beta. We can show by similar processes that \angle\gamma\cong\angle\sigma, so the theorem is proven.

subsection.p: A-B-C means that the points A,B, and C are colinear and B is between A and C.

statement.p: If a line \ell intersects a triangle \triangle ABC at a point D such that A-D-B, then \ell must intersect \overline{AC} or \overline{BC}.

proof.p: Assume there is some arbitrary triangle \triangle ABC with a point D such that A-B-D, with a line \ell that passes through point D. We apply the plane separation postulate using \ell as our line and the fact that a plane contains at least three non-collinear points. By the plane separation postulate, we can create two sets {A,B} and {C}. By the plane separation postulate, this means that segment \overline{AC} and \overline{BC} intersect the line \ell. Therefore, \ell must intersect \overline{AC} or \overline{BC}.

statement.p: If X is a point in the interior of \triangle ABC then ray AX intersects \overline{BC} at a point D such that B-D-C.
Two line segments are congruent (\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CD}) if and only if their measures (length) are equal (|AB|=|CD|).
A triangle is isosceles if and only if two sides are congruent.
In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are congruent.

proof.p: Consider \triangle ABC with AB \cong AC.
Draw an angle bisector from A to the base BC, meeting BC at point D.
\angle BAD \cong \angle CAD from the construction of AD.
AD \cong AD by the reflexive property.
\triangle ABD \cong \triangle ACD by the Side-Angle-Side congruence postulate.
Corresponding angles of congruent triangles are congruent, so \angle B \cong \angle C. Therefore, the angles opposite the congruent sides of an isosceles triangle are congruent.

statement.p: A point is on the perpendicular bisector of a segment if and only if it is equidistant from the endpoints.

proof.p: ( \Rightarrow ) Let \overline{BC} be a line segment. Construct a perpendicular bisector that intersects \overline{BC} at a point D so that B-D-C. Place a point A on this perpendicular bisector. By Axiom 1, we can construct unique line segments \overline{AB} and \overline{AC}. Since \overleftrightarrow{AD} is a perpendicular bisector to \overline{BC}, we have \overline{BD}\cong\overline{DC}. By reflexivity, \overline{AD}\cong\overline{AD}. In fact, since \overleftrightarrow{AD} is a perpendicular bisector of \overline{BC}, we know that m\angle ADB=m\angle ADC=\pi/2. Hence, \angle ADB\cong\angle ADC. By the SAS Postulate, \triangle ADB is in a one-to-one correspondence to \triangle ACD. So, \overline{AB}\cong\overline{AC} and therefore |AB|=|AC|, as desired.

statement.p: The supplementary angle formed by extending one side of a triangle is called an exterior angle.
The measure of an exterior angle of a triangle is greater than the measure of either of the opposing angles of the triangle.

proof.p: Suppose we have \triangle ABC. We can construct a ray from \angle ACB such that it goes through \overline{AB} and intersects it at point E, such that A-E-B and E is the midpoint of \overline{AB}. Thus, \overline{AE} \cong \overline{EB}.
By the Ruler Postulate, we then construct point F on the ray such that C-E-F, with E as the midpoint of \overline{CF}. Therefore, \overline{EF} \cong \overline{CE}.

By the Vertical Angle Theorem, \angle FEB \cong \angle AEC. Since \overline{CE} \cong \overline{EF} and \overline{AE} \cong \overline{EB}, it follows by SAS that \triangle AEC \cong \triangle FEB. Thus, \angle CAE \cong \angle EBF. By the Angle Addition Postulate,
m\angle ABD &= m\angle EBF + m\angle FBD
&= m\angle CAE + m\angle FBD
&= m\angle CAB + m\angle FBD.
By Axiom 12, m\angle FBD \ne 0.

statement.p: Two triangles are congruent if and only if all their sides and angles are congruent (\Delta ABC \cong \Delta DEF).

exercise.p: Determine if two triangles with two congruent sides and a congruent angle not between the two sides are congruent.

statement.p: Two triangles are congruent if and only if two corresponding angles and the side between them are congruent.
Two triangles are congruent if and only if two corresponding angles and a side not between them are congruent.

proof.p:
Suppose we have two triangles, \triangle ABC and \triangle DEF, with \angle BAC \cong \angle EDF, \angle ACB \cong \angle DFE, and \overline{AB} \cong \overline{DE}.
Assume, for contradiction, that m\angle ABC \gt m\angle DEF. We want to construct an angle \alpha such that \angle \alpha \cong \angle E. Using Axiom 18, we can construct a crossbar from \angle B that intersects \overline{AC}, constructing a point G such that A-G-C.

We now also have \angle \alpha \cong \angle E.
By doing this, through angle-side-angle, the \triangle ABG that we constructed is congruent to \triangle DEF and we have \angle AGB \cong \angle GCB \cong \angle DFE. But \angle AGB is an exterior angle of \angle BGC, by the exterior angle theorem, m\angle AGB \gt m\angle GCB and m\angle DFE which contradicts the definition of congruent triangles.

statement.p: Two triangles are congruent if and only if all three corresponding sides are congruent.

proof.p:
( \Rightarrow ) Construct triangles \triangle ABC and \triangle DEF such that
\overline{AB}&\cong\overline{DE}, \overline{BC}&\cong\overline{EF}, \overline{AC}&\cong\overline{DF}.
By the Angle Construction Postulate, we can construct a ray \overrightarrow{AP} such that m\angle PAB=m\angle FDE, where P and C are in separate half-planes separated by \overleftrightarrow{AB}. Then, on ray \overrightarrow{AP}, by the Ruler Postulate we can extend this ray and place a point F' such that \overline{AF'}\cong\overline{DF}. By Axiom 1, we can construct the line \overline{F'B}. Now, since \overline{AF'}\cong\overline{DF}, \overline{AB}\cong\overline{DE}, and \angle F'AB\cong\angle FDE, we know that \triangle ABF'\cong\triangle DEF by the SAS Postulate. For the sake of simplicity, we will re-label \triangle ABF' as \triangle DEF. So, we should have the following figure.
Essentially, we place \triangle DEF on \triangle ABC such that D overlaps A and E overlaps B. By axiom 1, we can construct the segment \overline{CF}.

We observe the new triangles \triangle CDF and \triangle CBF. Since \overline{AC}\cong\overline{DF} and \overline{BC}\cong\overline{EF}, triangles \triangle CAF and \triangle CBF are isosceles. By the Isosceles Triangle Theorem, \angle ACF\cong\angle DFC and \angle BCF\cong\angle EFC.

Since F lies in the interior of \angle ACB and C lies in the interior of \angle DFE, by the Angle Addition Postulate,
m\angle ACB&=m\angle ACF+m\angle BCF, m\angle DFE&=m\angle DFC+m\angle EFC.
Using the fact that \angle ACF\cong\angle DFC and \angle BCF\cong\angle EFC, we see that
m\angle ACB&=m\angle DFC+m\angle EFC=m\angle DFE.
So, we have that
\overline{AC}\cong\overline{DF},
\overline{BC}\cong\overline{EF},
\angle ACB\cong\angle DFE.
By the SAS Postulate, \triangle ABC\cong\triangle DEF.

( \Leftarrow ) Suppose \triangle ABC\cong\triangle DEF. Then, by definition, their corresponding sides are congruent. So,
\overline{AB}\cong\overline{DE}, \overline{BC}\cong\overline{EF}, \overline{AC}\cong\overline{DF}.

statement.p: Two right triangles are congruent if and only if two corresponding sides and a right angle not between those sides are congruent.

image.shortdescription: Image required for the proof of right angle side side theorem

proof.p: Take the above figure and suppose that line segments i and j to be congruent and the angles \angle CBA and \angle DBA to be congruent. Note that line segment f is congruent to itself. Then, per the Isosceles Triangle Theorem, \angle ACB\cong\angle ADB. Thus, by our congruences, we know that \triangle ABC\cong\triangle ABD per Angle Angle Side congruence.

statement.p: If two angles of a triangle are congruent then the sides opposite those angles are congruent.
If two sides of a triangle are not congruent then the angles opposite those sides are not congruent. Further the larger angle is opposite the longer side.
The sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is larger than the length of the other side.

proof.p:
Case 1: Where 1 side is longer than the others.
There exists some arbitrary triangle \triangle ABC. Assume that \overline{AB} is the longest side.
Subcase 1: |AB|+|AC| \gt |BC|
The length of \overline{AC} is a non-negative number and is being added to the longest side \overline{AB}. The sum will remain longer than the other side.
|AB| \gt |BC| then |AB|+|AC| \gt |BC| remains true.
Subcase 2: |AB|+|BC| \gt |AC|
Similar to Subcase 1.
Subcase 3: |AC|+|BC| \gt |AB|
Place a point D such that |AD|=|AC|. We need to show that |BC| \gt |DB| for the sum of the two sides to be greater than |AB|. By definition, \triangle ADC is an isosceles triangle and by the Isosceles Triangle theorem, the angles opposite the equal sides are congruent. m\angle ADC=m\angle DCA.
\angle ADC is an exterior angle to \triangle BDC and by the exterior angle theorem, m\angle ADC \gt m\angle BCD. \angle BDC is an exterior angle to \triangle ADC, so m\angle BDC \gt m\angle DCA. We know that \angle ADC\cong\angle DCA which means m\angle BDC \gt m\angle ADC but we also know that m\angle ADC \gt m\angle BCD. Therefore, m\angle BDC \gt m\angle BCD. By the extended inverse of isosceles triangle, |BC| \gt |DB|.
|AB|=|AD|+|DB| this equation becomes |AB|=|AC|+|DB|. Since we know that |BC| \gt |DB| this means |AC|+|BC| \gt |AB| which is what we wanted to prove.
Case 2: 2 or more sides are equal
This means for some \triangle ABC where |AB|=|AC|=|BC| then for the sum of any two sides, 2|AB| \gt |AB| which proves the theorem.

introduction.p: Each of the following is an equivalent Euclidean postulate.

ul.li: (Playfair) Given a line and a point not on that line, there exists exactly one line through that point parallel to the given line.
(Equidistance) Lines that are parallel are everywhere equidistant.
(Euclid) Given two lines and a transversal of those lines, if the sum of the angles on one side of the transversal is less than two right angles then the lines meet on that side.

subsection.title: Preparation
subsection.p: These theorems do not require a parallel postulate.

statement.p: If the alternate interior angles formed by a transversal of two lines are equal, then the lines are parallel.
The (shortest) distance between a point and a line is from the point to the foot of the perpendicular.
Given two lines and a transversal of those lines, if the sum of the angles on one side of the transversal is equal to two right angles then the lines are parallel.

subsection.title: Equivalency
subsection.p: The following theorem produces an easier to use version of Euclid's postulate.

statement.p: Euclid's postulate and Theorem are equivalent to the following. "The sum of the angles on one side of a transversal of two lines is equal to the sum of two right angles if and only if the lines are parallel."
Euclid's postulate implies Playfair's axiom.
Playfair's axiom implies the alternate interior angle converse theorem.

subsection.p: The alternate interior angle converse theorem states ``Given parallel lines and a transversal of those lines, the alternate interior angles formed by the transversal are congruent.''

statement.p: Playfair and the alternating interior angle converse theorem imply the equidistance of parallel lines.
The equidistance of parallel lines implies Euclid's postulate.
Prove the three postulates are all equivalent.

For \triangle ABC construct line \ell such that \ell \parallel \overline{AC} and B is on \ell. What is the relationship between the three angles at B (smaller than a straight angle) to the angles of the triangle?
The angle sum of the interior angles of a triangle is \pi.
The measure of an exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two opposing, interior angles.
A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if and only if both opposing pairs of sides are parallel.
Opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent.
If a transversal intersects three parallel lines in such a way as to divide itself into congruent segments, then any transversal of these parallel lines is also divided into congruent segments.
A line segment is an altitude if it connects a vertex of a triangle to the foot of the perpendicular on the opposite side.
Construct a triangle and enough parallel lines to divide one side of the triangle into four equal parts. Into how many parts do these lines divide the other sides?
The area of a triangle is equal to one half of the product of one side times the length of the altitude from the opposing vertex to that side.

introduction.p: Construct \triangle ABC. Construct \overline{DE} such that B-D-A, B-E-C, and \overline{DE} \parallel \overline{AC}.

statement.p: Construct \overline{AE} and \overline{EF} such that F is the foot of the perpendicular from E. Reduce the ratio of the areas of \triangle DEB and \triangle AED.
Construct \overline{DC} and \overline{DG} such that G is the foot of the perpendicular from D. Reduce the ratio of the areas of \triangle DEB and \triangle CDE.
Prove area of \triangle AED is equal to the area of \triangle CDE.
Two triangles are similar if and only if corresponding angles are congruent and the ratio of corresponding sides is constant.
A line parallel to one side of a triangle and intersecting the other two sides divides those sides proportionally.
A line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the triangle into two (whole and part), similar triangles.
Two triangle are similar if and only if they have three congruent angles.
Construct a definition for similar quadrilaterals. Construct examples to show that your definition works.
Explain why similarity is not defined simply as "all angles are congruent."
A line is a median if and only if it connects a vertex of a triangle to the midpoint of the opposing side.

subsection.title: Planar Transformations

statement.p: A function is a transformation if and only if it is one-to-one and onto.
A transformation is a planar transformation if and only if it is from \R^2 to \R^2.

subsection.p: For this course all transformations will be transformations of the Euclidean plane.

introduction.p: Describe the effect of each of the following transformations by considering the effects on the region (area) with the following vertices. (0,0), (2,0), (3,5), (0,4). Hint: map the vertices, then map the lines connecting the vertices.

statement.p: T_1:(x,y) \mapsto (y,x).
T_2:(x,y) \mapsto (x/2,y/2).
T_4:(x,y) \mapsto (\sqrt{x^2+y^2}x,\sqrt{x^2+y^2}y).
A transformation is an isometry if and only if \|P-Q\|=\|T(P)-T(Q)\|.

introduction.p: Determine which of the following transformations are isometries.

lemma.p: The composition of two isometries is an isometry.

statement.p: For any isometry T if A, B, and C are colinear, then T(A), T(B), and T(C) are colinear.
For any isometry T if A-B-C then T(A)-T(B)-T(C).
For any isometry T and any three points \triangle ABC \cong \triangle T(A)T(B)T(C).
For any isometry T and any three points m\angle ABC = m\angle T(A)T(B)T(C).
For any isometry T \ell_1 \parallel \ell_2 if and only if T(\ell_1) \parallel T(\ell_2).
For any isometry T circles are mapped to congruent circles.
A transformation is a dilation if and only if it can be defined by a point Z and a ratio k such that T(P)=Q where Z-P-Q and \|ZQ\|/\|ZP\|=k.
A transformation is a similarity if and only if it can be expressed as a composition of an isometry and a dilation.
For any similarity T, \|T(A)T(B)\|/\|AB\| =k.
For any similarity T if A, B, and C are colinear, then T(A), T(B), and T(C) are colinear.
For any similarity T if A-B-C then T(A)-T(B)-T(C).
For any similarity T and any three points \triangle ABC \sim \triangle T(A)T(B)T(C).
For any similarity T and any three points m\angle ABC = m\angle T(A)T(B)T(C).
For any similarity T \ell_1 \parallel \ell_2 if and only if T(\ell_1) \parallel T(\ell_2).
For any similarity T circles are mapped to circles.
The composition of two similarities is a similarity.

section.title: Analytic Transformational Geometry
section.p: The goal is to develop matrix formulas for arbitrary isometries using the basic isometry formulas given below as building blocks.

statement.p: A point with normal coordinates (x,y) is written (x,y,1) in homogeneous coordinates.

introduction.p: Goal: develop a rotation about a point [x_0,y_0]^T using the following steps.

task.statement: Find a transformation that moves [x_0,y_0]^T to the origin.
Find a transformation that moves [x_0,y_0]^T to the origin then rotates by \phi.
Find a transformation that moves [x_0,y_0]^T to the origin, rotates by \phi, then returns the origin to [x_0,y_0]^T.
State, using matrix notation, a transformation that rotates the plane about a point [x_0,y_0]^T by \phi.

An transformation T is a translation if and only if there exists a non-zero constant vector \vec{v} such that T(P)-P=\vec{v} for all points P.
An transformation T is a rotation if and only if there exists a fixed point C and constant angle \alpha such that m\angle PCT(P) = \alpha and \|\overline{CP}\| = \|\overline{CT(P)}\| for all points P

An transformation T is a reflection if and only if there exists a fixed line \ell such that the line perpendicular to \ell through P contains T(P) and the distances from P and T(P) to the \ell are equal.
Translations, rotations, and reflections are isometries.

statement.p: A covering of the plane is a tesselation if and only if it consists of a single shape infinitely reproduced using a finite set of transformations.
A covering of the plane is a tiling if and only if it consists of a finite set of shapes infinitely reproduced using a finite set of transformations.

description.p: A set of three line segments intersect to form an asterisk (sixty degrees between each line segment). At the tips of each of the six points of the asterisk, there is a star. The tips of the star curve slightly counterclockwise. This figure repeats indefinitely. left and right such that two, adjacent asterisks share one pair of stars. This asterisk figure also repeats indefinitely up-right and down-left (at sixty degrees) such that two, adjacent asterisks share one pair of stars.

figure.caption: Signature *236 (Variation on a Theme by Scott Roseman)

image.shortdescription: Signature *236 (Variation on a Theme by Scott Roseman)

description.p: The image consists of six cellos radiating outward as if they form an asterisk. The tops of the necks of each cello intersect in sets of three. The cello asterisks repeat indefinitely left and right such that two, adjacent asterisks meet at the tips of two of their necks. The cello asterisks also repeat indefinitely up-right and down-left (at sixty degrees) such that two, adjacent asterisks meet at the tips of two of their necks. In the space between the cello asterisks, are a set of four bass clefs mirroring each other at right angles. Lines indicate six fold mirror symmetry thru the center of each cello asterisk as well as three fold mirror symmetry through the meetings of the tips of three cellos. Another two fold mirror symmetry is between the bass clefs.

The image consists of pairs of french horn like shapes. Each pair are arranged so that the bells touch each other, but one is rotate 180 degrees from the other. These pairs fill a rectangular area. Those rectangles repeat indefinitely in a rectangular grid pattern. Left to right they repeat indefinitely by translation. Up and down they repeat by reflection. A horizontal line indicates the mirror symmetry. A symbol where the bells meet indicates the 180 degree rotational symmetry. The same symbol between two rectangular regions indicates another 180 degree rotation symmetry.

The image consists of a set of not fully opened tulips that repeat indefinitely in a rectangular grid. Each tuplip fits into a rectangle. Left to right the tulips repeat by reflection over a vertical line. Up and down they repeat by translation along with a relection over a vertical line thru the center of each tulip (a glide reflection). A vertical line indicates the mirror symmetry. A curved line from the tip of one tulip down to the tip of the tulip beneath indicates the glide reflection symmetry.

section.title: Hyperbolic Geometry
section.p: Hyperbolic geometry results by replacing the Euclidean parallel postulate with the following.

statement.p: Given a line and a point not on that line there exists at least two lines through the point and parallel to the line.
There were three major variants (wordings) of the Euclidean parallel postulate. Conjecture what these look like in hyperbolic geometry.

section.title: A Model for Hyperbolic Geometry
section.p: Hyperbolic geometry can be drawn with the aid of the Poincaré disc model. The hyperbolic plane is represented by a disc with the border not included ("open disc" in analysis terms). Lines are either diameters or circular arc that are orthogonal to the disc. The origin is the center of the disc. You will use the provided Geogebra file or one you search for online in Geoegebra with special tools to explore hyperbolic geometry.

section.title: Theorems of Hyperbolic Geometry
section.p: Note when working on these problems the model may be useful in figuring out why something works. However the proofs should be directly based on the axioms. It is legitimate to prove a statement using the model description if the model has been proven to be equivalent to the axioms. For this course proofs using the model will be worth fewer points than proofs directly from the axioms.

A point is an ideal point if and only if it is the intersection of parallel lines. These are sometimes called "points at infinity."
A line is the ideal line if and only if it consists of solely ideal points.

subsection.title: Axioms for Projective Geometry

ol.li: A line lies on at least two points.
Any two distinct points have exactly one line in common.
Any two distinct lines have at least one point in common.
There is a set of four distinct points no three of which are colinear.
All but one point of every line can be put in one-to-one correspondence with the real numbers.

subsection.p: The first four axioms above are the definition of a finite projective geometry. The fifth axiom is added for infinite projective geometries and may not be used for proofs of finite projective geometries.

statement.p: A line lies on at least three points.
Any two, distinct lines have exactly one point in common.
For any two distinct lines there exists a point not on either line.
There exists a one-to-one correspondence between the points of any two lines.
Every point lies on the same number of lines.
A projective plane in which each line lies on exactly $k+1$ points has a total of k^2+k+1 points and k^2+k+1 lines.
A statement is the projective dual of another statement if and only if one statement is obtained from the other by switching the roles of "point" and "line."
Each point is incident with at least three lines.
There exist four lines no three of which are coincident in a point.
There is a one-to-one correspondence between the real numbers and all but one of the lines incident with a point.
The projective dual of every projective theorem is also true.
Every line consists of the same number of points.
There exists a one-to-one correspondence between the lines thru any two points.

A transformation is a perspectivity if and only if it maps the points of a line to the points of another line such that all lines from points to their images are incident in a single point.

Draw two distinct lines. Choose a point not on either line. Choose three points on one of the lines and find the points on the second line to which they are mapped by the perspectivity defined by your chosen point.

A transformation is a projectivity if and only if it can be written as a composition of perspectivities.
A set of points is a triangle if and only if it is size three.
A set of lines is a trilateral if and only if it is size three.
Two triangles are perspective with respect to a point if and only if the lines connecting corresponding pairs of vertices are incident in a point.
Two trilaterals are perspective with respect to a line if and only if the corresponding sides are incident on a line.
Triangles perspective from a point are perspective from a line.
A projectivity is uniquely defined by three points and their images.

Given any two distinct points there is exactly one line that contains them.
Distance Postulate. To every pair of distinct points there corresponds a unique positive number. This number is called the distance between the two points.

li.p:
Ruler Postulate. The points of a line can be placed in a correspondence with the real numbers such that:
To every point of the line there corresponds exactly one real number.
To every real number there corresponds exactly one point of the line.
The distance between two distinct points is the absolute value of the difference of the corresponding real numbers.

ol.li: Ruler Placement Postulate. Given two points P and Q of a line, the coordinate system can be chosen in such a way that the coordinate of P is zero and the coordinate of Q is positive.
Every plane contains at least three non-collinear points.
Space contains at least four non-coplanar points.
If two points lie in a plane, then the line containing these points lies in the same plane.
Any three points lie in at least one plane, and any three non-collinear points lie in exactly one plane.
If two planes intersect, then that intersection is a line.

li.p:
Plane Separation Postulate. Given a line and a plane containing it, the points of the plane that do not lie on the line form two sets such that:
each of the sets is convex
if P is in one set and Q is in the other, then segment \overline{PQ} intersects the line.

Space Separation Postulate. The points of space that do not lie in a given plane form two sets such that:
Each of the sets is convex.
If P is in one set and Q is in the other, then segment \overline{PQ} intersects the plane.

ol.li: Angle Measurement Postulate. To every angle there corresponds a real number between 0^\circ and 180^\circ.
Angle Construction Postulate. Let AB be a ray on the edge of the half-plane H. For every r between 0 and 180 there is exactly one ray \overrightarrow{AP}, with P in H such that m \angle PAB=r.
Angle Addition Postulate. If D is a point in the interior of \angle BAC, then m\angle BAC = m\angle BAD + m\angle DAC.
Supplement Postulate. If two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary.

SAS Postulate. Given a one-to-one correspondence between two triangles (or between a triangle and itself). If two sides nd the included angle of the first triangle are congruent to the corresponding parts of the second triangle, then the correspondence is a congruence.
Parallel Postulate. Through a given external point there is at most one line parallel to a given line.
To every polygonal region there corresponds a unique positive real number called its area.
If two triangles are congruent, then the triangular regions have the same area.
Suppose that the region R is the union of two regions R1 and R2. If R1 and R2 intersect at most in a finite number of segments and points, then the area of R is the sum of the areas of R1 and R2.
The area of a rectangle is the product of the length of its and the length of its altitude.
The volume of a rectangle parallelpiped is equal to the product of the length of its altitude and the area of its base.

Cavalieri's Principle. Given two solids and a plane. If for every plane that intersects the solids and is parallel to the given plane the two intersections determine regions that have the same area, then the two solids have the same volume.
